title: Lesson 7: Working Together During Busy Periods
summary: Busy periods should bring out professionalism, not blame. Coordinate, communicate clearly, keep priorities and standards, and support colleagues without abandoning your own duties.

sections.title: Staff Development & Teamwork Training

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Cooperation, communication, time management, adaptability, emotional control, prioritisation and client service

sections.title: 1. Introduction: When everybody is busy, teamwork matters most
paragraphs: Imagine it is a Saturday afternoon at Zura Spa.
Several clients have booked massage sessions close to one another.
Two therapists are attending to clients.
Another therapist has just finished a session and needs to prepare her treatment room for the next appointment.
The receptionist is answering a telephone enquiry while another client arrives for a booking.
At the same time, a client calls to request a change in appointment time.
One therapist notices that fresh towels are running low.
Another employee needs clarification about the next available room.
Everybody seems to need something at the same time.
The receptionist becomes frustrated and says: "Can't you see I'm busy? Everybody should just sort themselves out!"
One therapist complains: "Reception never organises things properly."
Another responds: "That's not my problem. I've finished my own session."
The atmosphere becomes tense. Employees begin blaming one another. Communication breaks down. Clients notice the confusion.
Now imagine the same situation with a different approach.
The receptionist calmly informs the team about the arriving clients and appointment changes.
The therapist who has completed her session checks her next appointment and offers appropriate assistance.
Another employee promptly reports the towel shortage.
The supervisor clarifies priorities and coordinates available staff.
Everyone focuses on completing essential responsibilities while supporting colleagues where possible.
The spa remains busy, but the team stays organised.
The difference is not that one team has fewer responsibilities. The difference is how the employees cooperate under pressure.
At Zura Spa, busy periods should bring out the team's professionalism, not its worst attitudes.

sections.title: 2. What does working together during busy periods mean?
paragraphs: Working together during busy periods means coordinating responsibilities, communicating effectively and supporting one another when workload or operational pressure increases.
It involves recognising that the success of the team depends on how employees respond collectively.
Teamwork during a busy period does not mean everybody doing everything. It means everybody understanding what needs to be done and cooperating to achieve it.
list: Adjust the order of non-essential tasks.
Prioritise client safety and service quality.

sections.title: 3. Why busy periods test teamwork
paragraphs: It is often easy to appear cooperative when work is light.
There may be enough time to complete tasks slowly, discuss concerns and assist colleagues.
However, when several responsibilities arise at once, employees may become impatient or overwhelmed.
These situations reveal how well employees can manage themselves and cooperate.
An employee who is polite only when everything is going smoothly has not yet demonstrated consistent professionalism.
Professionalism is especially important when circumstances become demanding.

sections.title: 4. Why cooperation matters during busy periods
list: It reduces unnecessary delays. Clear coordination helps employees complete time-sensitive responsibilities efficiently.
It protects client experience. Clients receive more consistent attention even when the spa is busy.
It reduces pressure on individuals. Employees can request and provide appropriate support rather than struggling silently.
It prevents misunderstandings. Timely communication reduces confusion about appointments, rooms and responsibilities.
It helps maintain standards. Employees are less likely to overlook essential safety, hygiene and consent requirements.
It improves operational efficiency. Available time, rooms, supplies and staff can be coordinated more effectively.

sections.title: 5. Being busy is not an excuse for disrespect
paragraphs: Some employees become rude when they feel overwhelmed.
They may shout, use harsh words or speak impatiently to colleagues.
A receptionist asks a therapist: "Please, is Room 2 ready for the next client?"
The therapist responds: "Can't you see I'm working? Stop disturbing me!"
Although the therapist may be genuinely busy, the response is inappropriate.
Better response: "I'm still preparing Room 2. I expect it to be ready shortly. I'll confirm once the preparation is complete."
This response communicates the necessary information without hostility.
Pressure may explain why someone feels frustrated, but it does not justify mistreating colleagues.
Employees should remain respectful even when the workload is demanding.

sections.title: 6. The difference between being busy and being disorganised
paragraphs: A busy workplace has many responsibilities requiring attention.
A disorganised workplace may struggle because responsibilities are unclear, information is missing or tasks are poorly coordinated.
These situations are not the same.
Being busy is sometimes unavoidable. Being unnecessarily disorganised is something the team should work to improve.
table: Employees are unsure what to do first
Staff discover changes at the last minute
Several employees duplicate the same task
Employees argue or blame one another
Employees rush and overlook important steps

sections.title: 7. Understanding priorities during busy periods
paragraphs: Not every task should receive equal attention.
Employees should identify which responsibilities are most urgent and important.
A therapist has a client arriving in ten minutes.
A colleague asks her to assist with rearranging a supply cabinet.
The therapist should normally complete her essential appointment preparation first.
The supply cabinet can be addressed later unless it presents an immediate safety or operational concern.

items.label: 1. Immediate safety and client welfare
items.body: Respond to emergencies, unsafe equipment, hygiene hazards and concerns affecting client safety.

items.label: 2. Current and imminent client appointments
items.body: Attend to clients, confirm room readiness and complete essential service preparation.

items.label: 3. Time-sensitive operational coordination
items.body: Communicate appointment changes, resolve room conflicts and address shortages affecting upcoming sessions.

items.label: 4. Routine and deferrable tasks
items.body: Complete non-urgent stock organisation, administrative updates and other tasks at an appropriate time.

sections.title: 8. Communicating clearly under pressure
paragraphs: Busy periods require communication that is brief, accurate and respectful.
Employees should avoid unnecessarily long explanations when immediate operational information is needed.
Poor communication: "Nobody tells me anything around here. I don't even know what's happening with these appointments!"
Better communication: "Please confirm whether the 4:00 p.m. client has arrived and which room is assigned."
The second statement is specific and easier to act upon.
Clear communication saves time. Confusing communication creates more work.
list: Identify the relevant appointment or task.

sections.title: 9. The importance of quick team briefings
paragraphs: A short briefing can help employees prepare for a demanding period.

Supervisor: "We have several appointments between 3:00 p.m. and 6:00 p.m. Please confirm your room assignments and preparation requirements. Reception should communicate any appointment changes immediately. If there is a problem, report it early so we can coordinate."
This briefing can prevent confusion later.
A briefing should be focused and useful.
It should not become an unnecessarily long meeting that delays the work it is intended to support.

sections.title: 10. Supporting colleagues without abandoning your own duties
paragraphs: During busy periods, employees should be willing to assist one another.
However, assistance must be coordinated responsibly.

A therapist has finished her session. She has thirty minutes before her next appointment. Reception is busy, and another therapist needs help locating supplies. She checks her own preparation requirements and offers appropriate assistance. This is good teamwork.
Poor approach: A therapist abandons her current client or leaves essential room preparation incomplete to help with a non-urgent task. This creates another problem.
Effective support should reduce the team's workload, not simply move the problem from one employee to another.

sections.title: 11. Asking for help before becoming overwhelmed
paragraphs: Some employees wait until they can no longer cope before informing anyone that they need assistance.
This can create avoidable delays and mistakes.
A receptionist is handling several calls, two arriving clients and an appointment change. She becomes overwhelmed but says nothing. Important information is missed.
Better response: "I'm handling two arriving clients and several calls. Could someone available assist with directing the waiting clients while I complete the booking updates?"
This request identifies the situation and the specific help needed.
Asking for appropriate assistance is not a sign of weakness. It is a way of protecting service quality.
Employees should also respect colleagues who cannot immediately assist because of their own essential responsibilities.

sections.title: 12. Avoid unnecessary arguments during peak hours
paragraphs: Disagreements may arise during busy periods.
However, employees should avoid turning operational problems into personal confrontations.
A therapist discovers that the assigned room is not ready. She begins arguing with the previous therapist in front of clients. The argument delays preparation further.
Better approach: The employees should first identify what needs to be done to prepare the room safely.
If there is a disagreement about responsibility, it can be addressed through the appropriate supervisory process after the immediate issue is contained.
Delaying a personal argument is not the same as ignoring a serious safety concern.
Urgent risks must be addressed immediately.
During busy periods, prioritise solving the operational problem over proving who is right.

sections.title: 13. Maintaining emotional control
paragraphs: Pressure can influence emotions.
These feelings do not automatically mean an employee is unprofessional.
What matters is how the employee responds.
A receptionist feels overwhelmed by repeated calls. Instead of snapping at a colleague, she communicates the workload and requests support.
Emotional control means managing your response, not pretending you never feel pressure.

items.body: Recognise when frustration is increasing.
Avoid responding with insults or sarcasm.
Focus on the immediate responsibility.
Ask for clarification when necessary.
Request appropriate assistance.
Take an authorised short pause when needed and when client coverage permits.
Report workload concerns before they become serious.

sections.title: 14. Avoid rushing at the expense of quality
paragraphs: Busy periods can create pressure to work faster.
However, employees must not sacrifice essential standards simply to complete more tasks.
Efficiency means completing work well with minimal unnecessary waste. It does not mean cutting essential corners.
At Zura Spa, safety, hygiene, consent and professional boundaries remain important regardless of how busy the workplace becomes.
list: Reusing linen that should be replaced.
Shortening a client's agreed session without an authorised arrangement.

sections.title: 15. Handling appointment changes during busy periods
paragraphs: Appointment changes can affect multiple employees.
A client requests to move an appointment from 4:00 p.m. to 3:30 p.m.
The receptionist should not promise the new time without checking the necessary availability.
The change may affect therapist schedules, treatment-room availability, preparation time and other confirmed bookings.
Professional response: "Let me confirm therapist and room availability before I approve that change."
Once the change is authorised, relevant employees should receive accurate information promptly.
Do not create new scheduling problems by making commitments before confirming that they can be fulfilled.

sections.title: 16. Managing unexpected staff shortages
paragraphs: Sometimes an employee may be absent or unable to complete an assigned shift.
This can place additional pressure on the team.
A therapist becomes unavailable because of an emergency. Several appointments remain scheduled.
The supervisor must review available staff, room capacity and client commitments.
Employees may need to cooperate with reasonable, authorised adjustments.
However, they should not independently take on treatments they are not qualified to perform or accept unsafe workloads.
Teamwork during staff shortages requires coordination, not uncontrolled overloading of available employees.
list: Reassign duties within competence and agreed working arrangements.
Communicate necessary changes to affected clients.
Avoid pressuring employees to ignore safety or required rest.

sections.title: 17. The CALM method for busy periods
paragraphs: Several clients arrive close together.
The receptionist communicates the arrivals and confirms appointment details.
Therapists assess their schedules and prepare assigned rooms.
Available employees provide appropriate assistance.
The supervisor coordinates competing priorities.
Everyone maintains professional standards.
The workplace remains busy, but the team operates with greater control.

items.label: C — Communicate clearly
items.body: Share important information promptly and respectfully.

items.label: A — Assess priorities
items.body: Identify urgent responsibilities, client needs and safety concerns.

items.label: L — Lend appropriate support
items.body: Assist colleagues where possible without abandoning essential duties.

items.label: M — Maintain standards
items.body: Protect service quality, professionalism, hygiene, safety and accountability.

sections.title: 18. Knowing when to involve a supervisor
paragraphs: Two therapists believe they have been assigned the same treatment room.
Instead of arguing, they should promptly seek clarification.
Supervisors should help coordinate the team, but employees must also communicate problems early enough for coordination to be effective.
list: An employee is asked to perform duties beyond her competence.

sections.title: 19. What supervisors should do during busy periods
paragraphs: Supervisors have a responsibility to organise work fairly and effectively.
A busy workplace should not depend on employees constantly working beyond reasonable limits.
If high demand repeatedly overwhelms available staff, management should review staffing, scheduling and operational capacity.
list: Ensure client safety and service standards.
Review recurring problems after busy periods.

sections.title: 20. After the busy period: Review and improve
paragraphs: Once the immediate pressure has reduced, employees and supervisors should reflect on what happened.
The team discovers that treatment-room preparation was repeatedly delayed because clean towels were not replenished in time.
Rather than blaming individual employees immediately, the supervisor reviews the preparation and stock-check procedures.
The team agrees on clearer responsibilities and reporting arrangements.
A busy period should not only be something the team survives. It should also provide lessons that improve future operations.
list: What can be improved before the next busy period?

sections.title: 21. Practical case studies
paragraphs: Use the four case studies below in discussion. Identify the pressure, the unhelpful response, and the coordinated action the team should take.

sections.title: Case study A: The overwhelmed receptionist
paragraphs: Several clients arrive while the receptionist is handling telephone enquiries.
She becomes frustrated and begins speaking rudely to colleagues.
Expected lesson: Employees should communicate workload concerns and remain respectful under pressure.
list: What pressures is the receptionist experiencing?
Does the pressure justify rude communication?
What could the supervisor do to improve coordination?

sections.title: Case study B: The room conflict
paragraphs: Two therapists discover that they have been assigned the same treatment room.
Both have clients arriving shortly.
They begin arguing about who should use the room.
Expected lesson: Clear coordination and prompt escalation are more effective than personal arguments.
list: What is the immediate operational problem?
Who should clarify the room assignment?
How should the clients be kept informed if a delay becomes unavoidable?
What procedure could prevent similar conflicts?

sections.title: Case study C: The tempting shortcut
paragraphs: A therapist is preparing for another client.
She is running behind schedule and considers skipping a required cleaning step.
Expected lesson: Busy periods never justify ignoring essential hygiene or safety standards.
list: What should the therapist do instead?
How should the delay be communicated?
How can the team improve preparation efficiency without compromising hygiene?

sections.title: Case study D: The employee who refuses to help
paragraphs: A therapist finishes her assigned responsibilities and has sufficient time before her next appointment.
She notices that colleagues are struggling with several tasks.
She says: "I've done my own work. Everybody should do theirs."
Expected lesson: Employees should fulfil their own responsibilities while remaining willing to provide appropriate support.
list: What additional responsibility does teamwork create?
What reasonable assistance could she offer?
How might her attitude affect team morale?

sections.title: 22. Practical group activity: The busy Saturday simulation
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10–15 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise teamwork, prioritisation and communication during high-demand periods.

Scenario: It is 3:00 p.m. at Zura Spa. Several clients are expected within the next thirty minutes. Reception is receiving multiple calls. One treatment room is not ready. A therapist reports that clean towels are running low. A client requests an immediate appointment change. Another therapist has just completed a session and is preparing for her next appointment.

Group task: Assign participants the roles of receptionist, therapist, available support staff and supervisor. Ask them to decide what each person should do first, what information must be communicated and which tasks can wait.
Discuss which responsibilities should be handled immediately, which can be delegated and which can be postponed.
Expected outcome: Employees should demonstrate calm communication, appropriate prioritisation and coordinated teamwork.

items.label: 1. A client reports feeling unwell during a massage session.
items.body: Safety first. Stop the treatment, follow the emergency response procedure and obtain appropriate assistance. Do not continue because you are busy.

items.label: 2. A therapist needs to prepare for a client arriving in five minutes, while a colleague asks for help with a non-urgent stock arrangement.
items.body: Complete essential appointment preparation first. Help with the stock task later unless it is an immediate safety or operational concern.

items.label: 3. Reception receives a request to move a booking to an earlier time.
items.body: Do not promise the new time until therapist and room availability are confirmed. Then communicate the authorised change promptly.

items.label: 4. An employee notices that clean towels are running low before several appointments.
items.body: Report the shortage immediately so it can be coordinated. Do not wait until rooms cannot be prepared.

items.label: 5. Two employees begin arguing about who should prepare a room.
items.body: Stop the argument. Prepare the room safely, seek prompt clarification from the supervisor, and address responsibility after the immediate issue is contained.

items.label: 6. A therapist has completed her tasks and has time available while reception is overwhelmed.
items.body: Offer appropriate assistance after checking her own next appointment. Do not abandon upcoming duties, and do not refuse reasonable help merely because her own list is done.

sections.title: 23. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 7 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the most important principle when working together during busy periods? Everybody should focus only on personal duties / Employees should coordinate responsibilities and support one another appropriately / Employees should compete to finish first
What should an employee do when overwhelmed by several responsibilities? Communicate the workload and request appropriate assistance / Become rude to colleagues / Hide unfinished tasks
Which action is unacceptable even when the spa is extremely busy? Asking a supervisor to clarify priorities / Helping an available colleague / Skipping required hygiene or safety procedures

What should happen when two therapists are assigned the same room? They should argue until one gives up / They should seek prompt clarification and coordinate an appropriate solution / They should both promise the room to their clients
What does the CALM method stand for? Communicate, Assess, Lend support and Maintain standards / Complain, Argue, Leave and Mock / Compete, Accuse, Lose focus and Mislead

sections.title: 24. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what working together during busy periods means.
Describe five challenges employees may experience during high-demand periods.
Explain why being busy does not justify disrespectful communication.
Describe the difference between a busy workplace and a disorganised workplace.
Identify five benefits of effective teamwork during busy periods.
Explain how employees should prioritise responsibilities when several tasks arise at once.
Describe how a therapist can assist colleagues without neglecting her own appointments.
Explain why employees should request help before becoming overwhelmed.
Identify five workplace standards that should never be ignored because of time pressure.
Describe the CALM method in your own words.
Explain how supervisors can improve coordination during busy periods.
Identify three practical improvements that could help Zura Spa manage busy periods more effectively.

sections.title: 25. Seven-day teamwork under pressure challenge
table: Review your schedule and identify potential periods of high demand
Practise communicating urgent information clearly and respectfully
Offer appropriate assistance to a colleague during a busy period
Prioritise client safety and essential responsibilities
Avoid unnecessary arguments when operational problems arise
Apply the CALM method during a demanding situation
Reflect on what helped the team work effectively and what could improve

sections.title: 26. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Working together during busy periods is an important test of teamwork and professionalism.
At Zura Spa, employees should understand that high demand may increase pressure, but it should not destroy cooperation.
Busy periods require clear communication, appropriate prioritisation, emotional control and willingness to assist colleagues.
Employees should avoid blame-shifting, unnecessary arguments, rude communication and unsafe shortcuts.
They should remain accountable for their assigned duties while recognising that the success of the spa depends on coordinated effort.
Supervisors should also ensure that responsibilities are clearly communicated and workloads are managed fairly.
Next: Day 7 — Building a Winning Team, bringing together the lessons on teamwork, communication, respect, accountability and cooperation.

remember: The true strength of a team is not demonstrated only when everything is easy. It becomes visible when the workplace is busy, plans change and several people need assistance at the same time. At Zura Spa, pressure should not turn colleagues into competitors or make employees forget their professionalism. When the workload increases, communicate more clearly, cooperate more deliberately and remain respectful. Do not allow frustration to become an excuse for poor behaviour, and do not sacrifice client safety or service quality in an attempt to work faster. A strong team does not succeed because nobody experiences pressure. It succeeds because its members know how to support one another, remain accountable and work toward the same goal even when circumstances are demanding.
